newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW - Mongolia pushes for foreign investment.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Mongolia pushes for foreign investment.

text.p: Mongolia, in a bid to win more foreign investment, will keep pushing its commercial banks to meet international standards, Prime Minister Mendsaikhany Enkhsaikhan told Reuters Financial Television.

Mongolian authorities last year shut down two commercial banks in the former communist country, including the biggest, the People's Bank, in order to boost reforms of the nation's troubled financial sector.

"I believe our action will challenge other commercial banks to induce tougher discipline," Enkhsaikhan said in a recent interview. "If they do not work properly to meet international standards, I am not sure we wouldn't take such measures again."

Enkhsaikhan, who heads Mongolia's new democratic coalition government, is on an official five-day visit to Japan to celebrate the 25th anniversary of Mongolia-Japan relations, and to accept further grant aid from Japan.
He said a healthy financial sector was vital to attract foreign investment and added that international organisations were helping to send Mongolians to European countries for business training.
Last month, Mongolia became to first transition economy of the former Soviet bloc to join the World Trade Organisation.

The country aims to channel foreign investment into its copper, silver, gold and petroleum sectors and then create "a one-stop service to protect the foreign investor and to encourage greater transparency of Mongolia's legal and administrative framework," Enkhsaikhan said.

He said he also hopes for foreign investment following the announcement by the State Privatisation Committee last month that 129 shops, services and buildings in the capital, Ulan Bator, would be auctioned in February.

"Privatisation is one of our priority measures. But I stress it is a two-way street. We don't just offer assets for privatisation, we welcome proposals from foreign investors if they have an enterprise they wish to buy into," Enkhsaikhan said. "By the year 2000 we wish to privatise 60 percent of state-owned assets."
On the Mongolian economy, he said he was confident of achieving his GDP growth target of five percent in 1997, and between five and seven percent through to the next century.
Despite higher domestic energy prices, he said inflation was steady at 2.3 percent in January, the lowest since 1992.
"We can stabilise the economy on a macro level and thus encourage foreign investment," he said.
